title: How common each trait should be across a town
question: Across the few hundred people a player meets in one life, how common should each family of temperament traits be — which ones should turn up in most people, which in a handful, and which should be rare enough that meeting one is worth noticing?
whyItMatters: Every generated person currently draws every trait from one seeded curve, so each pole is equally likely on everybody and the population is uniform by construction. A count alone does not fix that: if a person carries two traits drawn from a flat list, a town of three hundred still has no texture, because the same traits recur at the same rate everywhere. Prevalence is what makes a neighborhood feel populated rather than sampled.
usableAnswer: A prevalence band per family in the catalog's fourteen — roughly what share of adults should be marked with something from it — with the rare ones called out by name, and a line on whether any of them should cluster by circumstance rather than being spread evenly. The reasoning behind each band matters more than its exact figure, because the figure becomes a pack value a modder can change.

sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Shows the single curve in use — [-2,-1,-1,0,0,0,0,1,1,2] — applied identically to every trait and every person. Nothing recorded says why that shape was chosen or whether it should differ per trait.

Asks how many traits one person should be marked with and whether that varies with age or recorded history. It is about one person; this is about the distribution across everybody, and neither answers the other.

sourcesChecked.source: docs/research/requests/ordinary-life-trait-set.json, filed by the people and life lane 2026-09-22
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Asks how large the vocabulary should be before entries stop being distinguishable. That is the size of the list. This asks how often each entry on it should appear.

notes: The three trait questions now open are deliberately separate and each can be answered alone: how large the vocabulary is, how many entries one person carries, and how often each entry appears. Answering any one of them is useful on its own.
A band is more useful than a number. A family that should appear in roughly a fifth of adults is actionable; 18.4 per cent is not, and would read as a measurement the game never made.

Clustering is worth a sentence if it applies. Some dispositions plausibly run in families or in a line of work, and the game already records both, so an answer that says where a trait concentrates can be used.
